title: They Lived to See the Promise
lead: Those who waited their whole lives saw the day come. God does not forget people who pray for the same thing for years.
questions: What have you been praying about the longest, and are you ready to keep waiting with God, like Simeon, without setting Him a deadline?
Has your knowledge of Scripture and of the Church’s affairs taken the place of a waiting heart, and how can you tell?
Which of the long-waiting, prayerful people in your community should you ask what they see before you plan the future?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Forty days after the night in Bethlehem, there are no more angels and no more shepherds. Mary and Joseph bring the Child to the temple and offer “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons,” the sacrifice provided for families who cannot afford a lamb. The Son of God began life in a family that paid the rate for the poor. In this scene the evangelist Luke singles out two people who recognize the Messiah in a forty-day-old Baby: Simeon and Anna.

Simeon “was waiting for the consolation of Israel,” and he had been given a promise the size of one lifetime: he would not die until he had seen the Messiah. In three sentences Luke mentions the Holy Spirit three times: the Spirit was upon him, the Spirit revealed it to him, and led by the Spirit he came, at the very moment “when the parents brought in the child Jesus.” A man who had let himself be led through years of waiting also let himself be brought to the one right minute. He takes the Baby in his arms and says: “Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace. For my eyes have seen Your salvation.” He did not see the end of the story, only its beginning, and that was enough for him. And in his song come the words we have been waiting for: this salvation is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles.” In a temple whose inner courts were closed to Gentiles, the most faithful of Israelites announces that the Child is for them too. The closer we are to God, the more room we see for outsiders.

Anna is there too: a prophetess, widowed after seven years of marriage, who for decades had not left the temple. She is the daughter of Phanuel, whose name means “face of God,” and she belongs to the tribe of Asher, which history had long since written off as lost. With God, neither tribes nor people get lost. It is she, an aged widow, who “spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem,” one of the first to bear public witness to Jesus. In this scene Luke gives special place to two old people, Simeon and Anna, who waited for the Savior with the Holy Spirit. Even the best knowledge of the letter cannot replace a waiting heart.

In yesterday’s reading the army of heaven sang over the fields of Bethlehem and the shepherds ran to the manger. Forty days later there is no trace left of that night. The angels have gone, the shepherds are back with their sheep, and Mary and Joseph are doing what every poor family in Israel did after a son was born: going to the temple to take care of the formalities the Law required. No one gives them a second glance. Hundreds of families just like them, with babies in their arms, pass through the courts. And in this ordinary, official scene two people are waiting who will recognize in a forty-day-old Child what no one else in the whole building noticed. This part of the series is addressed to those who have waited their whole lives. Today we meet two such people and learn their names.

sections.heading: The Offering of the Poor
paragraphs: Luke notes that Jesus’ parents brought “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” That detail says more than it seems to. After a birth the Law called for the offering of a lamb, but a family that could not afford a lamb was allowed to bring two birds. They used the rate for the poor. The Son of God began life in a family that had to be excused from paying the full price. And behind this humblest of offerings, interestingly, stood a whole infrastructure: across Judea archaeologists have excavated columbaria, underground pigeon farms with thousands of nesting niches carved into the rock. In one such cave, hidden in a pot, they even found Tyrian shekels, the currency of the temple tax. Breeding, transport, currency: the offering of the poor was an ordinary branch of the economy. Poverty in Israel was not an embarrassing exception that no one had written a procedure for. It was everyday life, and the Law had a separate, fully valid provision for it.

It is also worth reading carefully why this offering was made at all. The regulation concerns the mother’s ritual purification after childbirth, not moral guilt for having given birth to a child. Impurity after childbirth came from the natural, unavoidable course of life, and it was nobody’s offense. Mary is not bringing the birds to make up for some wrong. She offers them as a sacrifice because this is how the time after a child’s birth is brought to a close. That distinction is one we still need today: not everything that keeps a person out of the community for a while is their fault. Israel’s Law knew how to tell the difference. We don’t always.

sections.heading: A Man Who Knew How to Wait
paragraphs: Then Simeon steps onto the scene. Luke sketches him in three strokes: righteous, devout, and “waiting for the consolation of Israel.” That last phrase matters most. Behind the word “consolation” stands the Greek paraklesis, and Israel knew it from the book of the prophet Isaiah: “Comfort, comfort My people,” says your God (Isaiah 40:1). The consolation of Israel was not about lifting the mood but a concrete hope: that God would come and take up His people’s cause. John would later use this same word to form a name for the Holy Spirit: the Paraclete, the Comforter. So Simeon was waiting for what the whole Bible speaks about.

The man was given a promise cut to the measure of one life: “he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.” Notice how often Luke mentions the Holy Spirit here. The Spirit was upon Simeon, the Spirit revealed the promise to him, and led by the Spirit he came into the temple. Three sentences, and three times the word Spirit. And the fourth sentence is about timing: he came in just as “the parents brought in the child Jesus.” Not an hour earlier and not a day later. A man who had let himself be led through years of waiting also let himself be brought at that one right minute. The punctuality of this scene is not to Simeon’s credit; it is to the credit of the faithfulness of the One who had promised.

sections.heading: Now
paragraphs: Simeon takes the Baby in his arms and begins with the word his whole life had been working toward: “Now you are releasing your servant, Master, according to your word, in peace” (WEB). That is what a watchman hears when he is relieved after a long watch: your duty is done, you may go. The most astonishing part, though, is the reason he gives: “for my eyes have seen your salvation” (WEB). What exactly had those eyes seen? A forty-day-old baby of poor parents. No miracle, no throne, none of the things that were still to come. Simeon did not see the end of the story. He saw its beginning, and that was enough for him to die in peace. That says a lot about the nature of hope: it does not have to see everything. It needs to see enough to know whose hands hold the rest. It is also worth noticing one more thing: in this sentence salvation is not a concept or a doctrine. It lies in an old man’s arms, it breathes, and it has to be held carefully. Ever since God came in the flesh, we have come to know salvation face to face.

sections.heading: A Light That Belongs to No One
paragraphs: Then Simeon speaks of something we have been waiting for in this series for a long time. He speaks of the salvation “which You have prepared in the sight of all people, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel.” All people. The Gentiles. In a temple whose inner courts were closed to Gentiles, an old Israelite announces that this Child is for them too. Simeon did not invent this idea; he took it from the songs about the Servant of the Lord, who was to be a light for the nations. That had been Israel’s role from the start: a people chosen so that the light would travel onward, through them to everyone. History shows how easily the calling “a light for others” turns into “a light for us.” Simeon, a man of the deepest tradition, of prayer and of the Law, is living proof that faithfulness to your own heritage and a wide heart for outsiders do not merely coexist; they are tightly bound together. The closer we are to the God of Israel, the more room we see for those outside Israel.

sections.heading: A Sword in the Blessing
paragraphs: Simeon blesses the family, but he does not censor hope. He tells Mary hard things: this Child will be “a sign that will be spoken against”; because of Him many will fall and many will rise; “and a sword will pierce your soul as well.” A single speech holds both the light of the nations and a sword in a mother’s heart. This is an important feature of biblical hope: it does not rest on a promise that nothing will hurt. Simeon sees that around this Child “the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed,” that no one will be able to stay neutral about Him. A real encounter with God does not leave a person the way it found them: it lifts some up, lays others bare, and sometimes does both at once. Whoever promises people a faith that costs nothing is speaking of a different hope from the one Simeon held in his arms that day.

sections.heading: Anna Had Been There All Along
paragraphs: There is one more person in this scene. Luke writes: “There was also a prophetess named Anna.” Simeon came to the temple that day; Anna was simply there. “She never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying.” Her life story fits into two numbers: seven years of marriage, and eighty-four, which may be the years of her widowhood or her age. Either way, decades of loneliness prayed through in one place. Luke adds two details that are easy to miss. Anna is the daughter of Phanuel, and that name means “face of God.” In the form Penuel it was the name of the place by the Jabbok where Jacob, as we remember from day seven of our series, saw God face to face. The daughter of “God’s face” lived to see the day when she looked the Lord in the face quite literally. And the second detail: Anna comes from the tribe of Asher, one of the northern tribes carried off by Assyria seven centuries earlier and counted by history as lost. History wrote them off, but God evidently kept His books more carefully: on the day the Messiah appears in the temple, a daughter of a “lost” tribe is there too. With God, neither tribes nor individual people get lost.

And it is Anna, a woman, a widow, someone whose voice counted for little in that culture, who becomes the first person in Luke’s Gospel to tell others publicly about Jesus: she “spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.” The shepherds spoke about what had been announced to them; Anna speaks about Someone she has seen. An aged widow became the first evangelist before any of the Twelve had so much as learned to walk.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: Finally, notice whom Luke names as the ones who recognized the Child: Simeon and Anna. The Bible is silent about the scholars of Scripture who studied the Messiah every day. We do not know whether anyone else in the temple understood it at the time. The text highlights only the faithful waiting of Anna and Simeon, and the work of the Spirit. That is a lesson for us too, people who are often very well versed in the letter of the Law: knowing the regulations cannot replace a waiting heart. You can take care of God’s business and miss the God who is walking across the courtyard right now.

If you have been praying about the same thing for years and nothing changes, this story is for you. Anna waited for decades. About the length of Simeon’s waiting the text says nothing; we know only that he received a promise that he would see the Messiah before he died. God did not mix up the dates; He came at the right moment, just as He had promised. Your long waiting is not proof that He has forgotten you. Sometimes it is the place where He is preparing you for what He wants to show you. There is also a lesson here for us as a community: the Simeons and Annas are sitting in our pews. People who have prayed through decades sometimes see further than all our committees put together. Before we plan the future, it is worth asking those who have waited the longest what they see.
